Axios Future of Defense
By Colin Demarest · Sep 23, 2026

It's Wednesday. Again!

  • I just got back from Lynchburg, Virginia. More on that next week.
  • Also next week: some exciting news about the future of this newsletter. Stay tuned.

☎️ Situational awareness: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched Chinese officials a "notification mechanism" for AI incidents with national-security implications, my colleague Zach Basu reported.

  • More on those Cold War vibes, here.

What's happening: The Anduril Industries Armory, Saudi Arabian F-35s and HEO's $25 million round.

Today's newsletter is 1,572 words, a 6-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: "It was time"
 

An Atlas V rocket launches from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, in 2022. Photo: Ryan Quijas/DVIDS
 

Three U.S. military leaders in just as many days changed how the public talks about war in space, including the secretive weapons already among the stars.

Why it matters: Space fights will happen. They will look nothing like conflict on the ground or on the water. And the consequences will be enormous.

Driving the news: Last week and in quick succession:

  1. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said America has "on-orbit space control weapons" — a historic acknowledgment.
  2. Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess told reporters that "it was time" to have such a discussion and be clear-eyed about Russian and Chinese capabilities, including "being able to grapple a satellite and move it to a different orbit."
  3. And Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine said troops must be "prepared to fight, endure and win in global, contested environments, from the seabed to cislunar space."

Threat level: The U.S. has long held an advantage in space and has used the domain for surveillance, communication, missile tracking and more.

  • But experts warn Russia and China are eating into that lead.
  • The Pentagon's 2025 report on Beijing's firepower warned of "close approach and rendezvous operations between different sets of satellites" as well as "space-based jammers, including global navigation" spoofers.

Between the lines: Space is ruled not only by conventions and treaties but also social mores. Openly talking about weapons has been taboo, whether because of strategy, classification or stomach.

What they're saying: The pronouncements give "U.S. adversaries evidence for their claims that an arms race in space is already underway. But greater candor could also support negotiations if it leads to clearer doctrine and reciprocal transparency," Thomas González Roberts, the director of Georgia Tech's Engineering Space Policy Laboratory, told me.

  • "Space has been militarized for decades, and counter-space weapons are not new," he added. "The shift is toward more open acknowledgment."

Context: The U.S., Russia and China have all tested anti-satellite weapons.

What we're watching: If and when the Trump administration's ambitious space plans — Golden Dome, Space Academy, lunar reactors — are achieved.

Go deeper: Why D.C. defense experts wrestled with a simulated space nuke
 
 
2. Exclusive: Anduril's online arsenal
 

An EagleEye configuration, seen between then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll and Anduril Industries' Chris Brose. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios
 

Anduril Industries has quietly rolled out what it's calling Armory, a perusable database of drones, jammers, motors and other defense-tech products it has in hand, ready for sale and delivery.

Why it matters: This is Anduril's e-commerce moment — one that could boost business-to-business sales and build supplier relationships for the neo-prime.

  • "We're hoping we get a lot of original equipment manufacturer traffic and other types of A&D companies coming through," chief business officer Matthew Steckman told me.
  • "As a company, we've generally just gone after large, prime programs."

How it works: You can browse Armory right now.

  • Submitting an inquiry about any of the gear in stock — the Wisp sensor or Dive-LD undersea vehicle or Voyager chassis, for example — connects you to someone from Anduril to navigate the regulations and purchase.
  • "We have the demand coming in — orders booked," Steckman said. "But we're always building to a slightly higher rate than the orders booked, because the history of our business has told us to do that."

The intrigue: Missiles, like Barracuda, and other munitions were not listed on Armory as of last night.

Follow the money: Anduril was this year valued north of $60 billion. Backers include Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund and Thrive Capital.

  • The company is building the Fury robo-wingman for the U.S. Air Force, to fly alongside F-35s and F-47s, and recently expressed interest in the service's Massed Modular Aircraft effort.

The bottom line: "Coming up with the name Armory? As you can imagine, so many debates. So, so, so many debates," Steckman said.

  • "We're excited to see where it goes, and we're going to kick it into high gear."

3. Exclusive: Magnet-making moves
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

Vulcan Elements will make magnets for the U.S. Army's SkyFoundry initiative, which seeks stateside mass production of small drones, CEO John Maslin told me.

The big picture: Supply-chain surety is a national-security imperative.

  • China's rare-earth crackdown has strained manufacturers across the world while also complicating the relationship between Washington and Beijing.
  • "We won because we're decoupled," Maslin said of his startup's selection.

Zoom in: Vulcan will supply neodymium iron boron magnets for the service, which is closely watching the proliferation of unmanned battlefield technologies in Eastern Europe and the Middle East.

  • The magnets will support production of brushless direct-current motors.
  • "This is a major deal, if you believe drones are the future of warfare, delivery and agriculture," Maslin said. "Countries that make things win."

Follow the money: This marks Vulcan's 10th Defense Department contract.

Zoom out: Vulcan late last year secured a $620 million Office of Strategic Capital loan to "support the production of advanced rare earth element separation, metallization and magnet manufacturing capabilities."

  • The White House intervened to make it possible, ProPublica reported.
  • Vulcan responded yesterday to inquiries from the House Natural Resources and Oversight committees. A spokesperson separately told me that the startup maintains "it did not ask or solicit its investors to facilitate the Pentagon loan."

What's next: Vulcan is building a 1.1-million-square-foot facility in Benson, North Carolina, about an hour from Fort Bragg.

  • That footprint is equal to about 600 Waffle Houses, according to Maslin.
  • "Making these magnets is not easy," he said. "It's actually phenomenally complex."

4. ICYMI: Saudi F-35s
By Barak Ravid and Colin Demarest
 

A U.S. Air Force F-35A catches the sun over Farnborough Airport. Photo: Colin Demarest/Axios
 

The State Department approved the potential sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia at an estimated cost of $24.3 billion.

Why it matters: This major arms deal has been in the works for more than a year. If it goes through, Saudi Arabia would be the only Arab country that uses F-35s.

  • The Lockheed Martin-made warplanes would be a major technological upgrade for the Saudi Air Force and would raise questions about Israel's long-standing military advantage in the region.
  • The deal must go through a review by Congress and could still get stuck. Even if approved, it would take years before the first jets were supplied to the Saudis.

Driving the news: President Trump said before Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's visit to the White House in November that he approved of the deal.

  • Since then, the State Department has reviewed and negotiated the proposal.

What they're saying: "It's a categorically bad idea, until and unless the U.S. and [Saudi Arabia] agree to some concrete guardrails on Riyadh's defense and technological cooperation with China, more generally," Jonathan Ruhe, a fellow at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, told Axios.

  • The F-35, he added, is "a microcosm of a much larger problem in the relationship."

5. Quick hits
 

Illustration: Lazaro Gamio/Axios
 

📉 Nuclear security conditions in the U.S. and Russia are "dramatically declining," driven by the suspension of international cooperation and weakened oversight regimes, including at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, according to the NTI Nuclear Security Index.

  • Why it matters: "That's concerning, because those two countries have the largest responsibility — globally — for nuclear security, given the size of their arsenals and their stockpiles," NTI CEO Christine Wormuth told me.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: The report's most interesting finding may be about the emerging class of nuclear security leaders, which includes Australia, Ghana, Japan and the Netherlands.

🏗️ OpenWorks Engineering is opening a headquarters in Ashburn, Virginia, and planning a production facility in Detroit. The company, founded in the U.K., works on surveillance, counter-drone and other air-defense technologies.

  • Why it matters: "This expansion is a natural next step in our mission to continue to protect the territory and airspace of NATO nations and their allies," CEO Chris Down said in a statement.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Northern Virginia's lovely this time of year.

🔭 Australian startup HEO raised $25 million. It raised $8 million in 2023. Backers include Beaten Zone Venture Partners and Dcode Capital.

  • Why it matters: HEO uses "cameras and sensors attached to satellites to take 'flyby' images of other satellites and spacecraft in orbit," as my colleague Alex Fitzpatrick put it.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Space-domain awareness via startup? What a time to be alive.

⚙️ Lockheed Martin received its first batch of Patriot interceptor parts from GM Defense, less than a month after the two companies inked a contract.

  • Why it matters: Anything that gets PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancements going is a good thing. These parts generally "take months to years to produce," according to Lockheed.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Remember this?
 
 
6. Check this out
 

Tweetin' through it. Screenshot: @ZelenskyyUa/X
 

What interests me most about this post from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is not the footage.

  • Instead, it's the very specific list of weapons used, including Palianytsia.

The other side: President Trump on Truth Social said it was unfortunate that Russia "lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine."

  • He also called the conflict "ridiculous and never ending."
